parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define the $\textit{binding energy}$ of a nucleus.

markscheme_points.text: either (minimum) energy required / work done to separate the nucleons (in a nucleus) to infinity
or energy released when nucleons come together (to form a nucleus) from infinity

hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds protons and neutrons together in a tiny nucleus, and what you would have to do to pull them completely apart so they no longer attract each other.
Hint 2: Focus on the words minimum energy and the idea of moving nucleons to infinite separation, or reverse the idea to forming a nucleus from separate nucleons.
parts.proper_answer: The binding energy is the minimum energy required to separate all the nucleons in a nucleus to infinity. Equivalently, it is the energy released when separate nucleons join to form a nucleus from infinity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what binding means**
Think of the nucleus as tightly glued together by the strong nuclear force. Protons repel each other electrically, so something must be holding them. To break that hold you must do work on the nucleus.

Step 2: **Define it precisely**
Binding energy is that minimum work needed. Imagine taking every proton and neutron and moving them so far apart that they no longer interact - that is to infinity. So $$E_{B} = \text{minimum energy to separate nucleons to infinity}$$ The reverse is also true: if free nucleons come together from infinity to form a nucleus, this same amount of energy is released.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A stationary nucleus of uranium-238 ($^{238}_{92}\text{U}$) decays to form a nucleus of thorium-234 ($^{234}_{90}\text{Th}$). An $\alpha$-particle and a gamma-ray photon are emitted. The equation representing the decay is

$$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + ^{0}_{0}\gamma$$

The masses of the nuclei are given in Fig. 12.1.

{{figure:figure_12_1}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the relationship between the binding energies of the nuclei that is consistent with this reaction being energetically possible.

markscheme_points.text: (total) binding energy of thorium and helium (nuclei) greater than binding energy

hints: Hint 1: For any nuclear decay to happen on its own and release energy, the products must be more tightly bound overall than the parent was.
parts.proper_answer: The sum of the binding energies of the thorium-234 and helium-4 nuclei is greater than the binding energy of the uranium-238 nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link binding energy to stability**
A larger binding energy means more energy would be needed to break the nucleus up, so it is more stable. A spontaneous decay can only release energy if it goes to a more stable, more tightly bound state.

Step 2: **Apply to this alpha decay**
Here one parent $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$ becomes two product nuclei $^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$. For energy to be released, $$E_{B}(\text{Th}) + E_{B}(\text{He}) > E_{B}(\text{U})$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)1
parts.text: the change, in $\text{u}$, of the mass,
hints: Hint 1: Compare the total mass you start with to the total mass you end with using Fig. 12.1, remembering to add both product nuclei together.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find mass lost as energy**
Mass is not conserved in nuclear reactions. The missing mass $\Delta m$ becomes released energy. Calculate initial minus final: $$\Delta m = m_{\text{U}} - (m_{\text{Th}} + m_{\text{He}})$$

Step 2: **Insert the numbers**
$$\Delta m = 238.05076 - (234.04357 + 4.00260)$$ $$\Delta m = 238.05076 - 238.04617 = 4.59 \times 10^{-3}\text{ u}$$ The positive value shows mass has decreased.

parts.label: (b)(ii)2
hints: Hint 1: Recall how mass and energy are linked in relativity, and what conversion you need to change a mass in u into a mass in kg.
Hint 2: Convert $4.59 \times 10^{-3}\text{ u}$ to kg using $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and then use $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to find energy in joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert mass defect to kg**
You have $\Delta m$ in unified atomic mass units. To use $$E = mc^{2}$$ $m$ must be in kg. Use $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$: $$m = 4.59 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$$ $$m \approx 7.62 \times 10^{-30}\text{ kg}$$

Step 2: **Calculate energy in joules**
Now multiply by $c^{2}$ with $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$E = 7.62 \times 10^{-30} \times (3.00 \times 10^{8})^{2}$$ $$E \approx 6.9 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$$ This is the total energy released in one decay. An alternative route using $1\text{ u} = 931\text{ MeV}$ gives the same result, about $6.8 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: State and explain whether the energy of the gamma-ray photon is equal to the energy released in the reaction.

markscheme_points.text: Th nucleus / He nucleus / product nucleus has kinetic energy
energy of gamma photon must be less than energy released

hints: Hint 1: The parent uranium nucleus is stationary, so think about what must happen to momentum when the alpha particle shoots off in one direction.
Hint 2: Think about where the total released energy from (b)(ii)2 must go if the heavy thorium nucleus and the alpha particle both have to move, leaving what is left for the gamma photon.
parts.proper_answer: No, not equal. The thorium nucleus and alpha-particle recoil and so carry away some kinetic energy. Hence the gamma photon energy is less than the total energy released.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember momentum must be conserved**
The $^{238}\text{U}$ starts stationary with zero momentum. After decay the $\alpha$-particle moves off, so the $^{234}\text{Th}$ must recoil in the opposite direction to keep total momentum zero. Moving means both product nuclei have kinetic energy.

Step 2: **Share out the released energy**
The total $6.9 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$ is shared between kinetic energy of the massive particles and energy of the gamma photon: $$E_{\text{released}} = E_{k}(\text{Th}) + E_{k}(\alpha) + E_{\gamma}$$ Therefore $E_{\gamma}$ must be less than $E_{\text{released}}$.
